notes: Harker Experi(Mental): 18 teams, 21 rounds, guillotine, and the only league with IDP. Seven of fifteen starters are defenders — 47% of the lineup — because the D slot is a defensive flex, not a team unit. In this scoring (solo 2, assist 1, sack 6, TFL 2, pass defended 3) linebackers out-score the other groups at the top and do it with a tackle floor that shows up every Sunday, so the flex is a linebacker and the league needs 54 startable ones. The NFL produces about twenty who play every down, and the count falls each year as nickel and dime eat the base defence. That gap is the whole edge here. Defensive backs are the opposite: 36 needed against 64 starting safeties, so they wait — and pass defended at 3 makes the late ones better than the room thinks, not scarcer. Elimination is weekly, so floor beats ceiling everywhere: a sack-dependent edge rusher can post a zero, a hundred-tackle linebacker essentially cannot.

rules.label: RB-RB start
rules.note: Eighteen teams means replacement level is brutal everywhere. Anchor the backfield first.

rules.label: First linebacker by round 5
rules.note: Earlier than any public IDP advice, and right for this format. Five or six linebackers are genuinely every-down; eighteen teams are chasing them and the flex means most rooms want three. Wait until round seven and you are picking from the group with question marks — a rotational linebacker posts four points and four points from a starting slot is how you get chopped.

rules.label: Three linebackers by round 11
rules.note: Three, not two: the defensive flex is a linebacker in this scoring. Second by seven or eight, third by ten or eleven, and after that you are shopping for snap counts rather than names.

rules.label: First defensive lineman by round 10
rules.note: Sack at six plus tackle for loss at two keeps the top edge rushers worth real capital — but they score in lumps, and a lump that does not arrive is an elimination. Take one you actually like, then stop.

rules.label: Two defensive linemen by round 14
rules.note: For the second, weight snaps over sack totals: an interior lineman who plays early downs collects tackles every week, which is the half of the scoring that actually shows up.

rules.label: Two defensive backs by round 18
rules.note: The position to wait on, and six rounds later than this used to say. Thirty-six are needed against sixty-four starting safeties, so the twentieth is nearly the second — and those six freed picks are what pays for the earlier linebackers. Pass defended at three makes the late ones more valuable than the field thinks: take box safeties and slot corners who collect tackles and PD together, not shutdown corners nobody throws at.

rules.label: QB after the top two
rules.note: Not paying up for Josh Allen or Lamar Jackson.

rules.label: No one who will not play
rules.note: Elimination is weekly, so a pick that does not play in September may never play for you at all. Anyone carrying a real absence is kept off the board here. Questionable is not: fifty-nine ranked players carry it in August, McCaffrey and Chase among them, and acting on it would delete the top of the board — it is shown and left to you.

rules.label: Kicker last
rules.note: No team defence in this league — the D slot takes a defensive player, not a unit — so the kicker is the only mandatory pick left at the end.

note: No late-target rule here, unlike the other three leagues. Rookies and handcuffs are season-long bets, and this league eliminates the lowest scorer every week — a handcuff pays off in a week you may not reach, and the pool of eliminated teams' players hits waivers anyway, so bench depth is cheaper to buy later than to draft. Every pick has to score from week one. The D slot takes a seventh defensive player from any of the three groups; no deadline covers it, because a flex fills from whichever group is still worth taking and a rule naming one would be guessing.
